newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: U.S. sees no coherent plan yet for Zaire force.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sees no coherent plan yet for Zaire force.

text.p: The United States denied on Monday that it was blocking creation of an international force to aid refugees caught by fighting in eastern Zaire, but said it had still seen no coherent plan for assembling one.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Washington recognised that a force was needed, as demanded by a U.N. Security Council resolution on Saturday, which called on members states to begin preparations.
"The United States is not trying to block that force," Burns told reporters accompanying Secretary of State Warren Christopher to a conference in Cairo. "We are trying to help that force take shape."
France and other European states are pressing for urgent action to help at least one million refugees from Rwanda and Burundi caught up in fighting between Tutsi rebels and the Zairean army.

But the United States has been cautious. Burns rejected suggestions that a force could have gone in four or five days ago, saying U.S. military planners were still seeking answers to a series of questions.
"You can't go rushing in with troops without knowing what the mission is, the scope of responsibility and who's going to pay for it," he said.
Several conflicting plans were on the table, he said, adding that U.S. officials were discussing the various proposals with European and African countries.

Burns said lessons should be learned from past "mistakes" -- a clear reference to the U.N. mission to Somalia in 1993 which resulted in heavy casualties for U.S. and other forces involved amid charges that its original mandate had expanded.
The U.S. spokesman refused to say whether American troops would take part in an intervention force in Zaire, and if they did whether ground troops or just logistics forces would go.
"The answer is we have not yet made a decision... A decision has not been made because we don't have a coherent plan yet," he said.
U.S. officials said a decision would have to come from President Bill Clinton, who would review several options along with Secretary of Defence William Perry.

Burns said Washington continued to believe that the most urgent need was for Zaire and Rwanda -- whose troops have allegedly been aiding the Tutsi rebels -- to declare a ceasefire. But he said this was not necessarily a condition for an intervention force.
Richard Bogosian, the State Department's special envoy for Rwanda and Burundi, is currently in the Rwandan capital Kigali pursuing so far ineffectual efforts to stop the fighting.

Burns said it made no sense to try to force the refugees in eastern Zaire back into the camps from which they have fled, and Washington believed the Rwandans, who account for the vast majority, should be encouraged to return to their own country.
So far the refugees, mostly Hutus who fled Rwanda during an ethnic civil war there two years ago, have shown little inclination to return home.
